title: Human running performance from real-world big data
population: Wearable-tracker users: about 14,000 individuals, about 1.6 million exercise sessions (duration and distance), about 20 million km
findings: A previously validated two-parameter model (aerobic power index plus endurance index) was applied to real-world running activities of about 14,000 individuals with about 1.6 million sessions and about 20 million km.
The endurance index describes the decline in sustainable power with duration and gave 'a highly accurate race time prediction' (no numeric error in the abstract).
The model identified key parameters such as the lactate threshold.
Correlations between performance indices and training volume and intensity were quantified, 'pointing to an optimal training' (no values in the abstract).
A previously validated mathematical model was applied to about 1.6 million exercise sessions (duration and distance) from about 14,000 individuals, about 20 million km in total.
The model has two parameters: an aerobic power index and an endurance index (the decline in sustainable power with duration).
Including endurance gave highly accurate race-time prediction and identified key parameters such as the lactate threshold.
Correlations between the performance indices and training volume and intensity were quantified, 'pointing to an optimal training' (values not given in the abstract).
A previously validated two-parameter model (aerobic power index and endurance index) was applied to about 1.6 million exercise sessions of about 14,000 individuals (about 20 million km).

limitations: No numeric prediction error in the abstract; wearable data are self-selected without verified maximal efforts; applicability of the power-law/endurance model beyond marathon-range durations is not stated.
implications: Fit a per-athlete two-parameter model (aerobic power index plus endurance index) from the athlete's own best duration/distance efforts rather than a population-wide fixed exponent.
Store the endurance index as a tracked athlete parameter; a low index should lower predicted pace for long races.
Do not hard-code any training volume/intensity optimum from this paper.

Fit an athlete-specific two-parameter (power-like plus endurance-decay) model to logged duration and distance rather than a single race-time equation, and use it for targets at different race lengths.
Re-fit on a rolling window of recent activities so targets follow current fitness.
Do not hard-code a volume or intensity optimum from this paper.
A two-parameter (capacity plus endurance decay) model fitted to the athlete's own wearable data can derive pace zones and race predictions at any distance where a fixed exponent fails.
Refit continuously from recent best efforts so predictions track current fitness.
Do not use the cross-sectional volume-intensity correlations as causal prescriptions.

verification.notes: Crossref and Europe PMC re-fetched; findings match the abstract. 'Highly accurate' is the authors' phrase with no number, so no accuracy figure is asserted.
